newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin orders last troops out of Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin orders last troops out of Chechnya.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a major concession to Chechen separatists which smacked of a final acceptance of military defeat, on Saturday ordered all Russian troops to leave the rebel region.

His order cleared way for an interim cooperation agreement signed later in the day by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the head of the Chechen rebel government, Aslan Maskhadov, at a government dacha outside Moscow.

Withdrawal of all Russian troops from the region, devastated in 21 months of bloody fighting, was the main outstanding demand of the rebels, apart from their paramount desire to secede from Russia altogether.
Under the order, the last Russian units in Chechnya, Interior Ministry Brigade No 101 and army Brigade No 205, were to move out of Chechnya.
Yeltsin's decree, published by the Kremlin press service, did not state any deadline for withdrawal but ordered the government to organise it in a "planned manner".

The document, entitled "On measures to secure further peaceful settlement in the Chechen Republic", said it was aimed at "reaching accord in society, furthering a peace settlement and demilitarisation of the Chechen Republic".

"It is inarguable that the decree is a new confirmation of the president's view that there is no military solution to the Chechen conflict," Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a news briefing.

Yastrzhembsky said Russia felt it important to give the Chechen people a chance to make their choice "without being at gunpoint". But he added that the troops which would be withdrawn would stay close to the small region's borders.

Yeltsin's order and the Chernomyrdin-Maskhadov accord appeared to reflect a new Russian strategy of disengagement from Chechnya. Having failed militarily, Moscow is now keen to secure its interests in Chechnya through economic ties.

The agreement, defining the principles of relations between Russia and Chechnya for the period before January 27, when the breakaway region is due to hold elections, had much of the sound of an international treaty.

The text, published by Itar-Tass, said the two sides, using Russian and Chechen laws, had agreed to restore trade in goods and services by December 1 and work out customs regulations. Air, rail and road traffic is also to be restored.

Another agreement describing "special economic relations" between Moscow and Chechnya was to be worked out after the election in the region. Moscow has been mulling a proposal to make Chechnya a free economic zone.
More importantly, the two sides vowed to sign a special deal on the transport and refining of oil on Chechen territory. The rebel government promised to safeguard refineries and pipelines.

Diverted oil was a major source of income for Chechnya in the three years of self-declared independence before Moscow's 1994 assault. Although no longer a significant oil producer, the region occupies a strategic position between the rest of Russia and the oil-rich Caspian state of Azerbaijan.
The document said paying pensions, wages and compensation to those who suffered in the war was a priority for both sides.
Russia and Chechnya vowed "not to take any action threatening the security" of either side and to coordinate actions in the defence sphere.
After a breakthrough August 31 peace deal between Moscow and the rebels secured by now sacked Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed, Yeltsin said he opposed a hasty troop pullout.
But under that deal most Russian troops have already left Chechnya and the status of the two brigades that remained was one of the most contentious issues.
Moscow had wanted the two brigades to stay in Chechnya permanently but rebels insisted all Russian troops leave.

Despite improved relations between the two sides a permanent political settlement remains elusive, with the Chechen side insisting on full independence and Moscow trying to find a way of keeping the region within the Russian Federation.
